content: The following are professional descriptions of various studies and interventions related to nutrition, malnutrition, and child health: 1. An evaluation conducted in 2013 by Washington University School of Medicine focused on moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) and severe acute malnutrition (SAM) in Sierra Leone. 2. A pilot study in 2014 by Washington University and the University of Michigan investigated the use of PUFA-optimized ready-to-use therapeutic food (RUTF) for treating severe acute malnutrition. 3. Research by the United States Army Research Institute in 2015 assessed the efficacy of a calcium and vitamin D-fortified food product in improving bone microarchitecture. 4. A 2003 study by Universidad Autónoma de Querétaro and Procter & Gamble evaluated strategies to treat anemia in Mexican children. 5. A 2016 study by Jimma University and Nutricia Research examined the role of omega-3 long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs) in promoting healthy growth and development in infants and young children in Southwest Ethiopia. 6. The University of Oslo conducted a 2009 study on the effectiveness of supplementary feeding during infections in moderately malnourished children. 7. A 2009 study by the University of Copenhagen explored the role of essential fatty acids during complementary feeding. 8. A 2013 trial by the University of Oxford tested n-3 PUFA-enriched RUTF for childhood severe malnutrition. 9. A 2014 assessment by the University of Manitoba examined complementary feeding practices among Canadian infants. 10. A 2018 study by Hawassa University investigated the use of eggshell calcium to mitigate fluorosis in Ethiopia. 11. Michigan State University conducted a 2018 study on the feasibility and acceptability of a soy-fiber-maize complementary food in Malawi. 12. A 2020 intervention by the University of Cincinnati Children's Hospital focused on a Healthy Start to Feeding program. 13. A 2015 study by the University of British Columbia and Helen Keller International evaluated thiamin-fortified fish sauce to combat infantile beriberi in rural Cambodia. 14. The University of California, Davis, conducted a 2017 study on the acceptability and tolerance of proteinand micronutrient-fortified food products. 15. A 2018 study by the University of California, Davis, assessed a new food product for metabolically at-risk children. 16. The University of Colorado, in collaboration with the International Atomic Energy Agency, conducted a 2015 study on zinc bioavailability from amaranth-enriched maize tortillas. 17. A 2018 study by the University of Colorado examined the effects of protein from complementary foods on infant growth, body composition, and gut health. 18. A 2022 study by the University of Colorado investigated the effects of early complementary feeding on growth, neurodevelopment, sleep, and gut health. 19. A 2008 study by the University of North Carolina assessed the impact of yogurt containing BB12 on children's health and absenteeism in childcare. 20. A 2012 trial in the Democratic Republic of Congo evaluated the efficacy of caterpillar cereal as a complementary feeding option. 21. A 2019 study by the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology and Addis Ababa University examined iron status in Ethiopian infants. 22. A 2011 study in Denmark investigated the effects of vitamin D fortification of bread and milk on family health. 23. A 2009 study by the Hospital for Sick Children compared two feeding interventions for treating moderate acute malnutrition. 24. A 2010 study in Ghana evaluated the treatment of iron deficiency anemia in malaria-endemic regions. 25. A 2011 study in Bangladesh focused on preventing linear growth faltering among low birth weight infants. 26. A 2014 study by the United Nations World Food Programme assessed the acceptability of amylase porridges among children and caregivers. 27. A 2010 trial in Thailand tested the efficacy of iron, zinc, and vitamin A-fortified rice in children. 28. A 2012 study in Benin evaluated iron absorption from complementary food fortificants and their acceptability among children. 29. A 2013 study in Côte d'Ivoire examined the efficacy of iron-fortified complementary food and malaria prevention in young children. 30. A 2014 study in Kenya investigated iron absorption from rice fortified with ferric pyrophosphate. 31. A 2015 study in Senegal assessed iron absorption in mother-child pairs from wheat fortified with iron, with and without phenolic-containing beverages. 32. A 2015 study in Kenya evaluated the impact of iron and prebiotics fortification on infant health. 33. A 2020 study in Kenya examined iron absorption from wheat-based instant cereal using gut and stable isotope studies. 34. A 2011 study by PepsiCo assessed the bioavailability of iron from fortified oat drinks. 35. A 2007 study by the Research Institute of Child Nutrition explored modifications in complementary food composition to improve iron and fatty acid status in infants. 36. A 2021 study in Pakistan compared the treatment of SAM in children aged 6–59 months using RUTF and RUSF. 37. A 2014 study in Senegal evaluated the distribution of fortified yogurt to reduce anemia and improve milk supply. 38. A 2023 study by the USDA examined sustainable supplementation interventions to improve children's growth. 39. A 2016 study in Tanzania tested newly formulated fortified-blended foods for food aid. 40. A 2013 study in Burkina Faso assessed the impact of regular consumption of leafy vegetable sauces on children's micronutrient status. 41. A 2012 study in Kenya evaluated the effects of lactoferrin and dosing regimens on iron absorption from maize-based porridge. 42. A 2015 study in Cambodia tested the acceptability of a multiple micronutrient-fortified lipid-based nutrient supplement for children under two. 43. A 2011 study in Indonesia examined the effects of food-based interventions and psychosocial stimulation on growth and development in children under 24 months. 44. A 2018 study in Ethiopia explored barriers and enablers for scaling up community-based grain bank interventions for improved infant and young child feeding. 45. A 2012 study in Indonesia compared daily and weekly outcomes of supplementary feeding with locally produced ready-to-use food for mildly wasted children. 46. A 2018 study in Zambia assessed the impact of biofortified maize consumption on serum carotenoid concentrations in children. 47. A 2005 study in Malawi evaluated supplemental feeding with RUTF in children at risk of malnutrition. 48. A 2012 study in Vietnam examined the effects of two types of micronutrient-fortified complementary foods on growth in infants. 49. A 2009 study in Malawi assessed the post-intervention growth of children who received dietary supplementation with lipid-based nutrient supplements or maize-soy flour. 50. A 2017 study in Kenya and Cambodia analyzed constraints on field procedures for complementary food interventions.
